title: Photography direction for an independent hotel
metaTitle: Photography for an independent hotel site
excerpt: Photograph the room as a guest meets it. Lead with the doorway, not a drone shot of the pool, and write captions that admit the limit.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, objects shown so a person can tell what they actually are.
caption: The titles face the camera. Room photographs should face the guest the same way. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should hotel photography show first?
faqs.answer: The room from the doorway: bed, window, floor, and a sense of size. Shoot at a standing height and from the bed. A drone shot of the pool can live later, from a guest's height, if the pool is a real reason to book.

faqs.question: How honest does the light need to be?
faqs.answer: Honest enough that a guest recognizes the room at the hour they will see it. Correct a camera cast. Stop before the grade invents different paint or a wider floor. If the page says the room is small, the lens should agree.

faqs.question: What should alt text say?
faqs.answer: Describe the frame: the bed, the wall, the window, the bathroom door. Add a fact if the picture could mislead, such as a lane outside. Do not paste a slogan into the alternative. People who do not see the image still need the room.

markdown:
Independent hotel website photography has one standard: the picture should show the room as it actually is. A drone shot of the pool, used as the main argument, fails a traveler who is comparing three stays. The photographs are part of the decision, not a mood pasted under the headline.

WCAG treats images as content that still has to be perceivable when someone cannot see them, or cannot see them well. A room photograph needs a text alternative that says what the frame contains. web.dev's Core Web Vitals add a second, practical standard: the largest thing on the page, often that photograph, should paint within 2.5 seconds, and the page should stay visually stable, with cumulative layout shift at 0.1 or less. A beautiful file that arrives late, then shoves the date checker downward, fails the guest twice.

## The room is the argument

Choose the frame a guest gets when they stop in the doorway. The bed, the floor, the window, the far wall. That frame answers the question the other two tabs are also being asked: what is this room, really? If your best picture cannot be taken from the doorway because the room falls apart from there, the picture is not the problem. The listing is.

Shoot at a human height. Eyes of a person standing, and eyes of a person sitting on the bed. Those are the two positions that matter. A corner-of-the-ceiling angle is a trick to invent space. Travelers have slept in enough rooms to recognize it, and the ones who do not recognize it will feel the difference at arrival, which is the expensive moment to be honest.

Include the bathroom if the bathroom is part of the choice, and it usually is. A shower only, a tub that is short, a door that collides with the bed. Photograph the collision if it is real. You are not collecting evidence against yourself. You are declining to collect a complaint.

One room, told clearly, beats a montage of every corner of the property. The homepage can carry a single honest frame. Inner pages can carry the sequence: door, bed, window, bath. Sequence is an argument. Montage is a hope that feeling will replace sequence.

## What "as it actually is" requires

Light is part of the truth. Photograph the room at the hour a guest will see it, not only at the ten minutes when a west window looks like a postcard. If the room is dim at noon, a dim noon picture is the right picture. You can still turn on the lamp you actually provide. Do not add a lighting crew that will not be there on Saturday.

Color should match the paint. A grade that turns white walls blue, or wood floors orange, makes the other decisions on the page look slippery. Correct a color cast from the camera. Stop before you invent a different material. The traveler will hold the curtain up to the photograph in their memory and notice.

Scale needs a reference. A bed with no edge of the room in frame can be any size. Include a wall, a door, or the window so a person can estimate. If you state a fact in the caption, the picture should not contradict it. "Cozy" next to a wide-angle shot that doubles the floor area is a contradiction. Drop the lens, or drop the word. Prefer the lens.

People belong in the frame only when they are real and have agreed: the person at the desk, the cook at the pass, a guest who said yes and knows where the picture will go. A hired couple with a straw hat is a fiction. Fictions on a room page tax every true sentence around them.

Clutter should be the house's clutter, edited only for trash and for objects that identify a real guest without permission. A staged absence of every cord and every bottle looks like a catalog. A catalog is what the chain hotels already do, with a larger budget. Your advantage is a specific room. Do not sand it off.

## Why the drone shot of the pool fails

From the air, a pool is a blue shape and a roof. It does not show a bed. It does not show whether the water is two meters from the nearest guest's window. It does not show the chairs, the shade, or the fact that the pool is unheated and closed in October. As a lead image it answers a question the traveler is not asking first.

It also flatters the team. Drone footage looks like a finished brand. It photographs well in a pitch. The guest cannot sleep in it. When it opens the site, it spends the first glance on a shared cliché. The other independent hotel in the next tab may be making the same mistake. You win by not making it.

If the pool is a genuine reason to book, photograph it from the coping, at the hour you would sit there. Show how many chairs exist, not an infinity of water. Put that still on the page that discusses the pool, after the room has been established. Order is the direction. The pool can be true and still be second.

Reject cousins of the same shot. A lobby chandelier with no desk in frame. A linen detail so tight it could be any bed in any city. A flower arrangement that appears for the shoot and never for the guest. Details are allowed when the wider frame has already told the truth. Details instead of the wider frame are a hiding place.

Watch the selects with the sound of the street you can hear from that window, if you can do it on site. If the picture feels like a resort and the audio feels like a lane, believe the audio. Then either change the picture or change the words until they share a fact.

## A shot list for a comparison

You can direct a photographer with a list short enough to finish in a day. The list is the page outline, not a moodboard.

- The approach: the door from the street, in daylight, including whatever is ordinary and unpretty beside it.
- The arrival point inside: the table or desk where a person actually checks in.
- The priority room from the doorway, lamp on if that is normal, window as it is.
- The same room from the bed, so the guest's view is on the record.
- The bathroom, door position visible.
- Breakfast, if you serve it, with the number of seats that exist, not a table set for a fictional crowd.
- One constraint you are willing to talk about: the stair, the lane, the small shower.

That is a site. Extra frames are spares, not a second concept. Tell the photographer which frame is the lead before the shoot, so they do not spend the best hour on the roof.

Ask for files you can crop to the same aspect you will use on the phone. A lead that only works as a panorama will be ruined by the first screen of a mobile visit. Direct for that crop in the room, not afterward in a panic.

## What to refuse from the shoot

Refuse a lens that makes the room clearly larger than it is. Refuse a composite sky. Refuse to move the bed for the camera unless you will also move the bed for the guest. Refuse a style that requires a haze filter. Refuse people who do not work in the building, posed as if they do.

Refuse a usage story you cannot support. If the photograph shows a desk set for a full workday and the chair is decorative, you are photographing a service you do not have. The services page will have to contradict the picture, and the picture will win, because pictures are faster than paragraphs.

Refuse to let the pool open the edit just because it is the sharpest file. Sharpness is not relevance. The doorway frame can be the lead even when the drone file is technically cleaner. You are editing an argument, not a portfolio for the pilot.

Write the refusals down before the shoot, in the same note as the shot list. On the day, taste will lobby for the flattering frame. A written refusal gives the owner and the photographer a shared rule when the light on the water looks expensive.

## Captions, alternatives, and weight

Write the alt text as a description of the frame: "A double bed against the lane-side wall, with the window open and the bathroom door in the left foreground." Add the fact that protects the guest if the picture could mislead. Do not stuff a slogan into the alternative. WCAG's point is access to the content, and the content is the room.

Write a visible caption when the frame needs a time of day or a season. "October, 4 p.m." prevents a June booking made on a golden file. Captions can be short. They should not be punchlines.

Then make the file earn its place in the loading budget. The lead image is a likely largest paint. Export it at the size the layout uses, not at the size the camera captured. State width and height in the page so the date checker does not jump when the image arrives. web.dev's thresholds are a reasonable bar for that work: largest paint within 2.5 seconds, layout shift at 0.1 or less, measured for most users rather than on the office connection alone.

If a picture cannot hit that bar without looking soft, it is the wrong lead, or the page is carrying too many other scripts. Remove the film, the chat bubble, and the animation before you blame the photograph. A still doorway is usually light enough to be honest and fast.

## The phone will crop this

Every select should be checked inside a phone-shaped frame before you approve the set. The doorway picture that works on a wide screen often becomes a bed with no walls once the browser chops the sides. Direction includes that crop. If the honest part of the frame sits in the side that will be cut, recompose on site.

That check is the start of the mobile visit, which has its own rules for the first screen and the date control. [How the first phone screen has to hold the room and the dates](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-an-independent-hotel) is the next piece, because a correct photograph in a desktop-only layout still loses the traveler who never sees the desktop.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the selects before they become the site, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the doorway frame and the pool frame. The conversation is which one leads, and what the caption must admit.
